Split-Half Reliability for Network Estimates

Source: R/reliability.R
network_reliability.Rd

network_reliability() measures how much a network's weights depend on the particular sample: it splits the sequences (for an association network, the rows of its data) at random into two halves, estimates the network on each half with the original network's method and settings, compares the two weight matrices, and repeats this iter times. Each comparison gives four numbers: the mean, median and largest absolute difference between the halves' weights and their Pearson correlation, taken over all cells of the weight matrix. It takes one network or several, so the reliability of different methods or groups can be set side by side; a netobject_group contributes one network per group.

Each half holds only part of the sequences, so the agreement is that of networks estimated from a sample of that size. Differences are on the scale of the weights: counts of a "frequency" network and probabilities of a "relative" one are not comparable without scale. To see how far single edges move, use bootstrap_network(); to check centrality rankings, centrality_stability().

Usage

network_reliability(
  ...,
  iter = 1000L,
  split = 0.5,
  scale = "none",
  seed = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'net_reliability'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_reliability'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_reliability'
plot(x, bins = 60L, combined = TRUE, ...)

Arguments

...

The networks: one or more netobjects from build_network(). A netobject_group is split into its networks, named by group; an mcml is converted with as_tna() first, and a bare cograph_network is read as a netobject. Each network is named by its argument name or, failing that, its method; repeated names get a suffix ("_1", "_2", ...). A network without its sequence data (which build_network() keeps) raises an error, a network resting on one sequence an error of class nestimate_single_sequence, and networks of different methods with scale = "none" a warning. For the print(), summary() and plot() methods: ignored.

iter

The number of split-half iterations, at least 2. Default 1000.

split

The share of the sequences that goes to the first half, the rest forming the second, strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.5.

scale

The rescaling applied to both halves' weight matrices before they are compared, so that networks on different scales can be set side by side: "none" (default); "minmax", which maps each matrix to 0–1; "standardize", which subtracts the mean of its cells and divides by their SD; or "proportion", which divides by the sum of its cells. A matrix whose cells are all equal, or sum to 0, is left as it is.

seed

A seed for the random splits, so the result repeats exactly. The session's own random stream is left as it was. Default NULL.

x

For the print() and plot() methods: a net_reliability object.

object

For the summary() method: a net_reliability object.

bins

For the plot() method: the number of histogram bins per panel. Default 60.

combined

For the plot() method: TRUE (default) draws the four metrics as panels of one plot; FALSE returns a named list of four single-panel plots, one per metric, without drawing them.

Value

A net_reliability object. print() shows the mean and SD of each metric over the iterations, per network; summary() returns them as a data frame with one row per network and metric and the columns model, metric (mean_dev, median_dev, cor, max_dev), mean and sd; plot() draws their distributions. The object's fields:

iterations

A data frame with one row per iteration and network, and the columns model, mean_dev, median_dev, cor and max_dev.

summary

The table summary() returns.

models

The networks compared, as a named list.

iter, split, scale

The settings of the call.

print() returns its input invisibly. plot() draws the histograms (see Methods) and returns the ggplot invisibly; with combined = FALSE it returns, without drawing, a list of four ggplots named by the metric labels ("Max Abs. Diff.", "Mean Abs. Diff.", "Median Abs. Diff.", "Pearson").

Details

The first half holds round(split * n) of the n sequences (at least one), the second the rest; a split that leaves the second half empty (few sequences, split far from 0.5) raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input. For the transition methods ("relative", "frequency", "co_occurrence", and one-hot wtna networks, which are counted the same way), each sequence's transition counts are computed once and each half is summed from them, as in bootstrap_network(). Other methods are re-estimated on each half of the rows. The network's own scaling and threshold are applied to both halves. A half on which the estimator fails, or that loses a variable (a column constant in that half), gives NA for that iteration, counted in a warning of class nestimate_resample_failed. The summary leaves out missing values, such as a correlation that is undefined because one half's weights are all equal.

Methods

  • plot(): histograms of the split-half metrics over the iterations, one panel per metric, the mean marked by a dashed line and a label. With several networks, their histograms are overlaid, one colour per network, with a legend below.

See also

build_network, bootstrap_network

Examples

net <- build_network(data.frame(V1 = c("A","B","C","A"),
  V2 = c("B","C","A","B")), method = "relative")
rel <- network_reliability(net, iter = 10)
# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
seqs <- data.frame(
  V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE), V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE),
  V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE), V4 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, TRUE)
)
net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative")
rel <- network_reliability(net, iter = 100, seed = 42)
print(rel)
#> Split-Half Reliability (100 iterations, split = 50%)
#>   Mean Abs. Diff.     mean = 0.1537  sd = 0.0300
#>   Median Abs. Diff.   mean = 0.1329  sd = 0.0322
#>   Pearson             mean = 0.2006  sd = 0.1882
#>   Max Abs. Diff.      mean = 0.3760  sd = 0.0972
# }
